strengths: Well-motivated theoretical foundation leveraging recent insights (Stanczuk et al. 2024, Ventura et al. 2025) about score function Jacobians capturing manifold structure
Mathematically sound Riemannian metric construction with multiple interpretations (manifold-aware geodesics, pullback metrics through score space)
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across three diverse tasks (2D synthetic, image interpolation, video frame interpolation) with multiple metrics and datasets
Consistent improvements across FID, PPL, PDV, and RE metrics on all evaluated datasets
Requires no architectural modifications or additional training on pre-trained diffusion models
Thorough ablation studies and analysis of design choices (timestep selection, spectral gaps) with clear visualizations
Honest and transparent discussion of limitations and theoretical assumptions
Good reproducibility: code provided, detailed experimental setup, publicly available datasets
weaknesses: Incremental improvements over the most similar baseline (GeodesicDiffusion): ~3% on FID, ~5% on PPL—gains are consistent but modest given added computational overhead

Significant computational cost requiring 500 Adam iterations per interpolation path; no runtime comparisons provided; much more expensive than closed-form LERP/SLERP alternatives, limiting practical applicability
Limited scope: primary contribution restricted to interpolation; extensions to other metric-related tasks (clustering, etc.) deferred to future work, narrowing potential impact
Theoretical contributions are straightforward: Proposition 1 is intuitive once stated; using J^T J for metrics is conventional; novelty lies mainly in application context

Small experimental scale: only 50 image pairs per dataset; semantic similarity constraint (LPIPS < 0.6) excludes harder cases; critically, no human perceptual evaluation studies—all metrics are automatic proxies

Practical limitations undermine theoretical assumptions: non-symmetric Jacobian in practice claimed to satisfy Proposition 1 'approximately' without formal justification; spectral gap assumption only empirically validated, not guaranteed

Initialization and hyperparameter dependence: geodesic optimization requires good initialization (SLERP); timestep τ selection appears dataset-dependent (τ ∈ [0.4T, 0.6T]) with no principled selection method; regularization variant (G + λI) dismissed based on undescribed 'preliminary experiments'
Unable to operate at t=0 (clean data space) due to metric degeneracy, limiting applicability in certain scenarios
Presentation issues: key theoretical details relegated to appendices; Figure 1 is conceptual without clear before/after visual comparisons; pullback metric interpretation could be more prominent

strengths: Well-designed Riemannian metric derived from score function Jacobian with clear mathematical foundation and elegant spectral characterization of tangent-normal separation
Training-free approach applicable to pre-trained models without requiring additional training or architectural modifications
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (2D synthetic, image, video) with diverse metrics (PPL, PDV, FID, RE, MSE, LPIPS) and systematic ablation studies
Consistent practical improvements demonstrated across interpolation quality, guidance-corrected generation, and distillation with clear visual evidence of detail preservation
Thorough experimental documentation with extensive appendices covering alternative constructions, computational costs, hyperparameter sensitivity, and additional datasets
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core insight that score Jacobian separates tangent/normal directions derives from prior work (Stanczuk et al. 2024, Ventura et al. 2025), with this paper's contribution being primarily application to metric definition

Incomplete theoretical justification: no rigorous proof that geodesics under this metric optimize perceptual interpolation quality; relies on intuitive but unproven assumptions about manifold-tangent paths

Questionable metric reliability: requires τ > 0 (spectral gap collapses at t=0), Jacobian is only approximately symmetric with undefined behavior requiring regularization (Appendix B), and when these approximations hold is not characterized
Computational overhead significantly higher than closed-form baselines (Table 6); iterative optimization per interpolation path limits scalability and practical deployment

Modest empirical improvements on guidance correction (Table 4): marginal FID gains over CFG++ with statistical significance unclear; benefit appears to be preventing distortion rather than quality enhancement
Hyperparameter sensitivity with unclear practical guidance: multiple hyperparameters (τ, λ, CG iterations) with non-obvious settings and critical dependence on τ without principled selection strategy

Limited experimental scope: primarily 512×512 images without high-resolution testing; no comparison with recent diffusion-based or flow-matching interpolation methods or other geometry-aware approaches
Gap between theory and practice: multiple approximations (symmetric Jacobian, regularization requirements) and their cumulative effects not quantified; unclear when metric quality degrades

strengths: Well-motivated theoretical foundation connecting the Jacobian spectral structure to data manifold geometry through a principled Riemannian metric
Comprehensive experimental validation across multiple domains (2D synthetic, image/video interpolation on 7+ datasets) with consistent improvements and statistical significance testing
Thorough ablation studies on key hyperparameters (noise level τ, CG iterations, prompt adjustment) providing insights into method sensitivity
Strong qualitative results demonstrating preservation of fine details and natural transitions in interpolations
Clear mathematical exposition of the metric definition and geodesic-based algorithms with detailed appendices
weaknesses: Limited core novelty: primarily applies existing Jacobian observations (Stanczuk et al. 2024; Ventura et al. 2025) as a Riemannian metric; Proposition 1 is straightforward

Marginal practical improvements despite high computational cost: Table 2 shows gains <0.05 over FIM-based baseline; Table 6 indicates cost substantially higher than alternatives (N·S + T/ε + I + O(1)) making cost-benefit trade-off unfavorable

Weak theory-practice connection for guidance: tangent-normal decomposition is theoretically sound but its necessity for practical guidance is unclear; visual differences in Figure 8 are subtle and don't obviously justify added complexity

Incomplete theoretical justification: no formal proof that minimizing the metric improves interpolations; key claim that geodesics preserve endpoint probabilities lacks rigorous validation; assumption of Jacobian symmetry (Section B.1) is only approximate with unquantified impact

Hyperparameter proliferation without principled selection: τ=0.67 chosen empirically; CG iterations, prompt weight ω, and regularization λ require tuning; adds complexity for practitioners without clear guidance

Experimental concerns: most experiments on Stable Diffusion v2.1-base limiting generalization claims; differences from GeoDiff often <0.02 (within noise margins); guidance improvements may reflect implementation details rather than fundamental advantages; limited ablations on necessity of tangent-normal decomposition

Guidance correction questionable value: formulation (Eq. 5) mixes CFG scaling and metric decomposition with unclear contribution; Table 5 (distillation) suggests guidance can be absorbed without explicit metric—does student need metric decomposition?

Missing key comparisons: no comparison with recent guidance methods (e.g., Controlnet); no ablation removing tangent-normal decomposition entirely; unclear when metric-based guidance is necessary vs. when simpler approaches suffice

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: The insight that the Jacobian of the score function encodes data manifold geometry is clever and well-founded, with rigorous mathematical derivation.
Strong mathematical foundation: Clear connections to differential geometry, proper proofs (Proposition 1), and elegant formulation of the Riemannian metric.

Comprehensive experimental validation: Extensive experiments across multiple domains (synthetic data, 4 image interpolation datasets, 3 video benchmarks) with proper statistical significance testing (p < 0.01).
Training-free practical method: Applicable to pre-trained models without modification or additional training, enabling immediate real-world deployment.
Thorough ablation studies: Detailed analysis of hyperparameter sensitivity (spectral gap τ, regularization λ, CG iterations) demonstrating robustness and providing insights.
Excellent presentation: Clear writing, effective geometric visualizations (Figures 1-4), and good balance between mathematical rigor and intuition.
Consistent improvements: Statistically significant gains across multiple metrics and datasets (e.g., best FID and RE scores on image interpolation, best MSE and LPIPS on video).
weaknesses: Computational overhead under-addressed: DDIM inversion, multiple score function evaluations, and iterative optimization add significant cost; no wall-clock time comparisons or real-time deployment feasibility analysis provided.
Incremental improvements in primary application: Image interpolation gains are modest (~1-2% on PPL, marginal on FID/PDV/RE), though guidance correction shows stronger improvements.

Jacobian symmetry assumption insufficiently justified: Critical assumption in Section B.1 lacks empirical validation across datasets; no analysis of approximation error or failure modes when J_θ is not symmetric.

Limited application scope demonstrated: Only two applications (interpolation and guidance correction) shown; broader utility of discovered geometry unexplored; no investigation of other manifold operations.
Manifold existence assumption under-examined: No discussion of when low-dimensional manifold assumption breaks down; real-world data may not satisfy this uniformly.
Hyperparameter selection lacks guidance: Spectral gap τ requires task-specific tuning (0.67 for images vs 0.47 for video) with no principled selection method for new datasets.
Sparse discussion of failure modes: Missing analysis of when staying tangential might be suboptimal or when the method should not be applied.
Missing recent comparisons: Several recent manifold-aware and geometry-aware diffusion methods not compared; incomplete coverage of related geometric approaches.
